nameStory: Basil-thyme gets its name from its delightful scent that reminds people of thyme, one of our favorite cooking herbs. When you crush the leaves between your fingers, you'll catch that familiar, aromatic fragrance that makes you think of Mediterranean gardens. It's also called spring savory, hinting at both its early blooming time and its savory, herb-like smell.
description: Basil-thyme is a small, mat-forming herb that's part of the mint family, though it's much less common than its famous cousins. This low-growing perennial typically reaches about 8 inches tall and spreads about a foot wide, creating neat little patches. Like other mints, it has the characteristic square stems and opposite leaves, but it stays much smaller and more compact than most of its relatives. The tiny flowers and subtle thyme-like fragrance make it a charming find for plant enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats about 8 inches tall and 12 inches wide, staying much smaller and more compact than most other mints you'll encounter

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers typical of the mint family, with two lips and delicate petals that appear in clusters along the stems

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, opposite leaves arranged in pairs along the square stems, releasing a faint thyme-like scent when crushed between your fingers

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that you can feel by rolling them between your thumb and finger - a classic mint family trait that feels distinctly four-sided rather than round

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Distinctive thyme-like fragrance when leaves are bruised or crushed, much more subtle than strong-scented mints but clearly herbal and pleasant

habitat: Basil-thyme prefers sunny, open areas with well-drained soil, often found in rocky or sandy locations where other plants struggle. Look for it in disturbed sites, field edges, and areas with thin soil that get plenty of direct sunlight. With only 3 recorded observations in New England, it's quite rare in our region and most likely found in scattered locations with the right sunny, well-drained conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges and the plant begins to spread, with the thyme-like scent becoming noticeable as leaves develop. Early flowers may appear toward late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period when the small tubular flowers are most visible and the plant reaches its full spreading size of about 12 inches across.
seasonality.fall: Plants may continue flowering into early fall, with the mat-like growth habit still clearly visible and leaves retaining their characteristic scent.
seasonality.winter: As a perennial, the plant dies back but the root system survives underground, ready to emerge again in spring.

funFact: This tiny herb serves as a food plant for the caterpillars of Coleophora tricolor, a small moth whose larvae actually live inside rolled-up leaves, creating their own little sleeping bags from the very plant they're eating!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small mints, but basil-thyme's low, mat-forming habit and thyme-like scent set it apart from the taller, more aggressive spreading mints. Remember: if it smells like thyme and stays under 8 inches tall, you've probably found basil-thyme rather than a true mint.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, basil-thyme isn't closely related to either kitchen basil or thyme - it just happens to smell similar to thyme. This naming based on scent rather than botanical relationships is common with aromatic plants and can be confusing for beginning botanists.
compareHints: Basil-thyme stays much smaller and more compact than its cousin wild basil, which can grow several feet tall. Lesser calamint is closer in size but lacks the distinctive thyme-like scent that makes basil-thyme so recognizable. Think of basil-thyme as the 'miniature mint' of the calamint group - same family traits, but in a much smaller, ground-hugging package.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild basil differs from its calamint relatives by having much denser, more compact flower clusters that sit directly against the stem.
Lesser calamint differs from wild basil by its much smaller, greyer leaves and stronger oregano scent rather than basil-like fragrance.
